did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a musical heading—“To the leader: Do not destroy”—and is attributed to Asaph; it is described as both a “psalm” and a “song.”
Did you know? From the very beginning of the psalm, thanksgiving to God is emphasized, connected with the story of his wonders and the nearness of his name.
Did you know? This verse says that judgment will take place at the time appointed by God, who presents himself as the one who will judge fairly—that is, with justice and integrity.

Did you know? The description of the earth melting and its pillars trembling emphasizes the fragility of the world, while God’s words present him as the one who establishes and upholds its foundations.
Did you know? The expression “to the boastful” refers to those who behave arrogantly or boastfully, and the verse warns them not to exalt themselves.

Did you know? “Lifting up the horn” is an image of power, status, and pride; therefore, the warning not to lift up the horn or speak with an “arrogant neck” is a warning against self-exaltation and boastful speech.
Did you know? The psalm mentions the east, the west, and the wilderness, teaching that judgment determining a person’s fate comes from no human source or geographical direction.
Did you know? The explicit conclusion is that God is the judge: he humbles one person and exalts another, so a person’s status is not determined solely by personal strength or initiative.
Did you know? “The cup of the LORD” is described as wine filled and mixed, from which the wicked drink down to its dregs; it is a vivid image of judgment that cannot be escaped.
Did you know? The psalm ends with a clear contrast: the horns of the wicked will be cut off, while the horn of the righteous will be lifted up—a picture of power being turned in favor of justice.
